2.13.1.en: If the pagan cold of winter turned man into stone, then the divine Word, "the Sun of Righteousness", has risen, turning the frozen stone into warm waters, as the psalmist says: "Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters". He has raised up children to Abraham from stones (Mt 3:9).

2.13.2.en: In this spring which the Lord made (by His resurrection), the divine Word calls His bride to arise, saying to her: "Arise, my near one, my fair one, my dove, and come away" [10]. Here the call is directed to the bride to arise and to advance in the way of perfection, just as the Lord said to the paralytic: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk" (Mt 9:6). The Word did not ask him only to take up his bed but commanded him to walk, and I think that by walking He meant here advancement and growth in perfection. Here too He commands His bride: "Arise, and come away"... This command carries a power which the Bridegroom gives His bride to arise and to walk in the way of perfection.

2.13.3.en: As for His calling her "my near one, my fair one, my dove," the words came in a precise order, and as St. Gregory says: [Observe the order of the words, how each word is connected with the one before it. See how the thought came linked together as in a chain. The bride hears the commandment, and it carries the power of accomplishment by the Word: she arises, then she advances, and becomes fair, then she is called a dove. For how can you see a beautiful image in a mirror unless the mirror receives the reflection of a beautiful form?! So also with the mirror of human nature: it cannot become beautiful unless the Beautiful One (God) draws near to it, and it is formed by the image of the divine beauty. When our human nature fell to the earth and looked upon the serpent, it bore its image. And now it arises and looks upon the Good, turning its back to sin, and bears the image of the Good which it faces, as it now looks at the original beauty, that is, the dove. As it turns toward the light, it bears the image of the light, and through this light it bears the form of the beloved dove, I mean the dove that symbolized the presence of the Holy Spirit].

2.13.4.en: This is the secret of bearing fruit in the spring: by His resurrection He drew near to us and we drew near to Him (my near one), and we bore His beauty within us (my fair one), so we became His dove (since the Holy Spirit dwelt in our inner life).

2.14.s.en: Repetition of the call to resurrection:

2.14.0.en: The Lord repeats the call to His betrothed to arise, saying to her:

2.14.1.en: "Arise, and come away, my near one, my fair one, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the strongholds.

2.14.2.en: Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" [13-14].

2.14.3.en: Why does the Suitor repeat the call to His bride to arise? St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, answers, saying: [He calls the bride who has arisen to arise again, and her who has drawn near to Him to come to Him... for it is fitting for her to go from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and she is always looking at what she is, so she sees herself as far less than she wishes to be. So although she is a "dove" by her perfection in Christ, He commands her again to become a "dove," that is, to enter into a more perfect state, and while she is standing, He calls her to arise, giving her power to arise continually and for a life of growth and progress.

2.14.4.en: The first time He calls her to arise and come to Him: "Arise... and come away"; but now He calls her to go out from her house and from her city and to set out to the clefts of the rock, to the covert of the strongholds. For since the time of winter, in which the bride had shut herself in, has passed, she must now go out and depart, not only from the evil lusts of the flesh but from the whole visible world... He calls her to meet with Him within the eternal, invisible fortresses!

2.14.5.en: If the Apostle saw in the rock which followed the people of old the person of Christ Himself (1 Cor 10:4), then the Bridegroom here asks His bride not only to go out from herself and from the visible world but rather to enter into Christ Himself, the true Rock, so that she may live with Him without veil or covering... but she beholds His glory with open face (2 Cor 3:18), and speaks with Him.

2.14.6.en: Her entering the rock to meet with the Bridegroom indicates her security, for there the ancient serpent cannot find a path, as it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: the way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock..." (Prov 30:18). Origen comments on this, saying: [There is no path for the serpent (on the rock), that is, there can be no trace of sin on this rock which is Christ, for He alone is without sin. So when souls benefit from taking refuge within this rock, they go in peace to the place of the strongholds, that is, they enjoy contemplation of eternal, incorporeal things].

2.14.7.en: David spoke of this rock in another figurative way in the Psalm: "He set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings" (Ps 40:3). Do not wonder if the rock is for David like ground or a foundation on which the soul walks toward God, while for Solomon it is the covering set over the soul so that it may enjoy the inner mysteries of wisdom, for the Lord Christ Himself was once called the Way (Jn 14:6) in which the believers walk, and at another time He was called the Forerunner, as Paul says: "Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus" (Heb 6:20).

2.14.8.en: In the same way came God's word to Moses: "I will put thee in a clift of the rock... and thou shalt see my back parts" (Ex 23:22-23). This rock is Christ; it was not completely closed but had a cleft, and (at the same time) this cleft of the rock is also He who reveals God to men and makes Him known to them, since no man knows the Father save the Son (Mt 11:27). No one sees the back parts of God, that is, the things that happen in the last times, unless he enters into the cleft which is in the rock, that is, learns them through the revelation of Christ Himself.

2.14.9.en: Therefore Christ's call to the soul to arise is a call to enter into Christ Jesus so as to meet with God with open face... "Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice."

2.14.10.en: This saying does not mean that her face is hidden from Him or her voice unknown to Him, but He wants her to enter into union with Him, so that she appears before Him with the boldness of love as a bride who appears without a mask, and speaks in complete frankness.!

2.14.11.en: Origen comments on this call, saying:

2.14.12.en: [Here under the covering of the rock the Word of God calls the soul that has become His near one to enter into the strongholds, which, as we have said before, means contemplation of the eternal, invisible things. There He says to her: "Let me see thy countenance." For surely there is no longer any trace of the old veil that was upon her face, but she has come to contemplate the glory of God without fear, saying: "And we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth" (Jn 1:14)].

2.14.13.en: And when she becomes worthy that what was said of Moses be said of her: "Moses spake, and God answered him" (Ex 19:19), His saying is fulfilled in her: "Let me hear thy voice." Truly, what great praise she enjoys when it is said to her: "Sweet is thy voice!" David, the very wise father, also said so: "My meditation of him shall be sweet" (Ps 104:34). For the voice of the soul is sweet when it speaks the word of God, and expounds the faith and the teachings of truth, and reveals God's dealings and His judgments. But if foolish talk comes out of the mouth, or elegant jesting, or trifles, or idle words for which she will give account in the day of judgment (Mt 12:36), then this voice is neither sweet nor delightful. Christ gives no ear to such a voice! Therefore the perfect soul sets a watch before her mouth and a fortified door upon her lips, so that what she utters may be seasoned with salt, with grace toward those who hear it (Col 4:6), and then the Word of God says: "Sweet is thy voice."

2.14.14.en: He says also: "And thy countenance is comely." You can discern what kind of "countenance" this is which the Word of God praised and described as comely, if you understand what Paul meant by the countenance when he said: "But we all... with open face beholding" (2 Cor 3:18), and also: "but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). It is without doubt a kind of countenance that is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), after the image of Him that created it (Col 3:10), having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and without blemish, like the Church which Christ presents to Himself (Eph 5:27); in other words, it means the souls that have attained perfection, those which form the body of the Church. This body truly appears beautiful and comely when the souls of which it is composed persevere in obtaining the beauty of perfection. For just as the soul, when it is agitated, distorts the form of the bodily face and makes it provoking, but when it is calm gives the face a form that carries peace and gentleness, so also the face of the Church is beautiful or ugly according to the character and aspirations of the believers. It is written: "A cheerful countenance is a sign of a heart that is in prosperity" (Sir 13:26), and in another place it is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" (Prov 15:13). The heart is joyful when the Spirit of God is in it, whose first fruit is love and the second is joy (Gal 5:22). And I think that worldly wisdom took its ideas from these truths when it said that the wise man is beautiful and every wicked man is ugly.

2.14.15.en: It remains for us to give a lengthy explanation of "the covert of the strongholds." For this expression, as we said before, means the presence of a wall before a wall, and this is what Isaiah expressed: "salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks" (Isa 26:1). The wall signifies the city, and the other wall which is before the first or around it signifies greater and stronger fortifications. And the Word of God calls the soul and leads her out of her bodily concerns and sensory perceptions and brings her out to teach her the mysteries of the other life, so that she is in a fortress, in order that, as she is strengthened and surrounded by hope in the eternal things, no bait draws her away and no trials disturb her.

2.14.16.en: Thus the call of the Lord Christ to the Church or to the human soul for the experience of resurrection is a call to set out from the human self and to depart from bodily things, and to cross over to the new heavenly life... It is an entrance into "the covert of the strongholds," that is, into the bosom of the heavenly Father in which the Church is fortified as the dove of Christ. Thus Christ who rose from the dead wants to enter with His believers into the bosom of His Father and to reveal to them the divine mysteries, as He says to them: "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (Jn 1:18). Again He says: "for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 15:15), and also: "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me" (Jn 17:24).

2.14.17.en: He calls her to union with Him, "the true Rock," and to enter with Him into the bosom of His Father, "the covert of the strongholds," to be with Him forever... These are the eternal fortresses which bestow beauty on the Church, so that her voice is sweet and her countenance comely.!

2.14.18.en: Thus the Suitor calls His betrothed to fly from the realm of carnal thought to spiritual thought, so that she may no longer be "a silly dove" (Hos 7:11) but He sees her meek and pure, and longs for her prayers and her clinging to Him... He sees her face continually and hears her voice.

2.15.s.en: He warns her against the slanderers

2.15.0.en: If the "Word of God" has come down to man, stretching out His hand to him, and man has received Him, He returns to warn him against the slanderers, who work to destroy the union of God with the believing man, saying:

2.15.1.en: "Take (seize) us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes (have blossomed)" [15].

2.15.2.en: In His repeating the word "foxes" there is a warning against them, for they creep lightly and enter through small holes to spoil the vineyard at the beginning of its growth... By this they spoil huge quantities of the coming fruit; although they are small, they spoil man's growth and maturity.

2.16.0.en: 1. If we take this warning as directed from the Lord Christ to the believer or to the soul that is joined to her Christ, then these little foxes may be sins which we consider slight, such as the white lie or jesting... They may be witty friends or certain books or a certain place... Therefore it is fitting for us to keep all our inner doors closed against any little fox, abstaining from all appearance of evil (1 Thess 5:22).

2.16.1.en: Origen sees that these little foxes [are the opposing powers of the demons which destroy the flowers of the virtues in the soul and scatter the fruit of faith through the corrupt thoughts and misleading notions which they instill]. He also says: [Surely at the moment of sin, some evil spirit is present in the heart of man, and there he works. We allow him to enter and receive him within us by our evil inclinations].

2.16.2.en: And as St. Mark the Ascetic says: [Satan offers us small sins that seem trivial in our eyes, because without this he cannot lead us to great sins]. 2. If we take this warning as directed from the Lord Christ to the Church, Origen says: [These words appear to be directed to the teachers of the Church, so the commands are given them to catch the foxes that spoil the vines. Here the foxes are understood as the teachers who promote heretical doctrines, those who mislead the hearts of the simple and spoil the vineyard of the Lord so that it does not bring forth the blossom of Orthodox faith, using their embellished arguments. Therefore the commands are given to the teachers of the Catholic Church to hasten to rebuke these foxes and resist them while they are still small and beginners in their corrupt teachings, and to subdue the opponents of the word of truth and take them captive by showing the truth].

2.17.s.en: The little foxes in the Holy Bible:

2.17.0.en: It is written in the Book of Psalms: "But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth. They shall fall by the sword: they shall be a portion for foxes (jackals)" (Ps 63:9-10). These are the wicked teachers who wish to deceive the soul, so they push it to destruction with vain embellished words; they use earthly, temporal wisdom, so they take the souls of the righteous into the lower parts of the earth instead of lifting them up toward the eternal and heavenly things, and they make their own souls and the souls of those whom they teach a portion for the foxes (evil teachings or demons) instead of being the portion of the Lord. To such as these the Lord says: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Mt 8:20). The Lord finds no place in their hearts to rest, but the demons (the foxes) rest, and their souls turn into dens for them.

2.17.1.en: Since Herod became misleading, the Lord also called him a fox (Lk 13:31).

2.17.2.en: And in the Book of Judges we find Samson who caught three hundred foxes and took firebrands and turned tail to tail and put a firebrand in the midst between every two tails; then he set the brands on fire and let them go into the standing corn of the foreign pagans, and burnt up both the shocks and the standing corn, with the olive yards (Judg 15:3-5). He represents the true and faithful teacher who knows how to gather all the heresies and tie their tails together, showing the heresies' opposition to one another, and when he kindles in them the fire of truth, the fields of evil, innovations and heresies are burnt up.

2.17.3.en: And in the Book of Nehemiah Tobiah the Ammonite stands mocking what Nehemiah was doing, saying: "Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall" (Neh 4:3). This is a symbolic picture of what the world does when it sees the walls of the Gospel raised up with the believers, the living stones who have gone out from the captivity of sin to become a wall and a temple at a heavenly level. The world mocks, saying that the Gospel was not established on earthly philosophical foundations, supposing that any fox or earthly argument is able to demolish it.!

2.17.4.en: The Holy Bible has taught us to beware of the little foxes but not to fear them, for we have been given power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Lk 10:19)... We say in Christ Jesus: "Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones" (Ps 137:9), the Rock. For we strive to destroy evil from the beginning of its going forth and to bury it under the feet of Christ our Rock.

2.18.s.en: The hunters of the little foxes:

2.18.0.en: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that the hunters of the little foxes are the angelic powers or the company of the holy Apostles: 1. Perhaps they are the angelic powers who accompany the Lord in His descent to earth and work for the sake of His Kingdom, for it was said of the Lord that He is "strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle" (Ps 24:8). 2. They may represent the Apostles who were sent to hunt such beasts of prey out of the hearts of men, to make a place for the Son of man in which to lay His head.

2.19.0.en: By the divine Incarnation the Suitor came down to His betrothed to ask for her hand, and by His resurrection He called her to arise in Him and with Him, so that she does not fear death nor dread the authority of sin, but He asked her to beware of the foxes that spoil the vineyard of union with Him. The bride responded to the repeated call of the Suitor "Arise... come away," so she entered the wedding banquet, which is His crucifixion and resurrection, to enjoy union with Him, and she communed with Him, saying:

2.19.1.en: "My beloved (my near one) is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.

2.19.2.en: Until the day break (breathe), and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved (my near one), and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether (the narrow mountains)" [16-17].
